messages.author: dbc05514efb8c1db
messages.subject: Re: P-value inflation problem
parts:
Hi Stan users

 

I’ve been using a Poisson regression to model the noise in count data arising from a next generation sequencing technique. I’m trying to identify events more extreme than the background (noise). I’ve been using a Poisson p-value to identify such events. I have a plot of log2 fold change of the observed count divided predicted count verses predicted count. From the plot, I have a p-value inflation problem. Too many events with a low Poisson mean are being called statistically significant at 1% FDR threshold. I do believe the Poisson regression is a good model for this data. I’ve done ten-fold cross-validation to evaluate the model’s performance on held-out data, and I do get a median Spearman correlation of 85%. I wanted to try the Bayesian posterior predictive p-value. That is, to generate yrep[i] ~ poisson(lambda[i]), and then calculate b.pvalue[i] ~ step(yrep[i] – y[i]) – 0.5*ifelse(yrep[i]-y[i]==0,1,0). My assumption is that posterior predictive p-value might be more stringent frequentist p-value. Does anyone give some advice on this problem?

 

Best,

Mark

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: P-value inflation problem
parts:
I can't really address your stats question, but once
you have lambda[i], can't you just generate the expectation
rather than sampling? It'd be more efficient inferentially.

And in Stan, instead of

step(yrep[i] - y[i])

you can just write

(yrep[i] > y[i])

which takes on value 1 if condition is true and 0 otherwise.

Similarly,

ifelse(yrep[i] - y[i] == 0, 1, 0)

can be replaced by just

(yrep[i] == y[i])

which is 1 if they're equal and 0 otherwise. That is, the conditions
act like they have indicator functions wrapped around them arithmetically.

- Bob
